source: Mandel, Karvetski, Dhami (2018) Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: what works, what fails (Judgment and Decision Making 13(6))
finding: Verified from the full PDF. 50 UK intelligence analysts judged which of 4 exclusive tribes (A-D) a target belonged to. Their stated probabilities did not sum to 1. Forcing them to sum to 1 (coherentizing) cut error. Averaging the 50 coherentized judgments cut it further.
numbers: Mean absolute error (MAE) vs the Bayes-correct values: raw 0.23 [0.21,0.26]; coherentized 0.15 [0.13,0.18], a 35% reduction, d=0.96, t(49)=6.77. Coherentize then equal-weight average of all 50 analysts: MAE 0.09, a 61% reduction. N=50, one fictitious case, 12 probabilistic cues, tribe base rates 5/20/30/45%.
quote: This represents a 35% reduction in MAE and approximately a 1 SD improvement.
limits: The 61% needs a crowd of 50; one analyst gets 35%. The 'correct' answer is a computed Bayes value, not a real outcome. Rank correlation of analyst judgments with correct values was weak (about 7% shared variance), so coherentizing fixes sum errors, not understanding. Human analysts, not LLMs. Mean experience 14 months.
agent_relevance: Closes the 'unverified 35 and 61' flag. For G5, the 35% is the transferable number (single judge, normalise to sum 1). The 61% is an aggregation gain, a different operation.

source: Mandel et al. (2018) JDM, footnote 4 and Discussion: normalisation versus quadratic-programming coherentization
finding: Plain normalisation (divide each stated probability by their sum) did slightly better than the closest-coherent-vector method. Coherentizing helped the ACH group about twice as much as the control group. The ACH checklist method itself did not help accuracy.
numbers: Normalisation MAE 0.13 vs 0.15 for the quadratic-programming method (Jon Baron's analysis, footnote 4). Effect of coherentizing: d=0.69 control, d=1.37 ACH. ACH vs control accuracy: d=0.45 favouring control (probability of superiority .62). After coherentizing the tradecraft effect was 0.01 [-0.04,0.07].
limits: One vector of correct values, one task: the authors say the study is not designed to compare methods. The 0.13 vs 0.15 difference is not tested in the text I read. The gain depends on analysts being over-sum (unpacking effect); a judge whose sums are already near 1 gains little.
agent_relevance: Directly supports 'plain code normalisation is enough, no fancy coherentization needed'. Also warns: the gain scales with how incoherent the raw numbers are, so log the sum of the model's raw scores.

source: Gigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995) How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: frequency formats, Study 1 (Psychological Review 102)
finding: Primary paper opened. Study 1: 60 students, 15 inference problems, each in probability and frequency format. A Bayesian algorithm was counted only when both the process and the outcome were right. Frequency formats roughly tripled the rate for the standard menu.
numbers: Study 1 (N=60, 15 problems, two sessions): Bayesian algorithms in probability format 16% (standard menu) and 28% (short menu); frequency format 46% (standard menu) and 50% (short menu).
quote: elicited 16% and 28%, for the standard menu and the short menu
limits: Strict joint criterion (reasoning process plus numeric outcome). Students from 10 disciplines at Konstanz, not experts. Paper and pencil. Frequency 'format' is entangled with the 'menu' (which numbers are given); the paper tests that in Study 2.
agent_relevance: RESOLVES the clash: 16% vs 46% is the standard menu; 22% vs 48% is the average of the two menus ((16+28)/2 and (46+50)/2). Both numbers are right and describe different cells.

source: Gigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995) Study 2 (N=15): probability formats and information menus
finding: Study 2 used 15 students and 24 problems. Probability-format scores were lower than in Study 1, but the gap between menus stayed. A short menu, which makes the Bayes computation simpler, beat the standard menu.
numbers: Study 2 (N=15, 24 problems): Bayesian algorithms in probability formats 6.4% (standard menu) and 17.5% (short menu). Menu gap about 12 points in both studies. Bayesian algorithms almost doubled from standard to hybrid menu and almost tripled to the short menu (Table 4).
limits: Very small N (15). The authors' account is computational simplicity of the arithmetic, not an innate frequency mind; later work disputes the mechanism (Cui 2023 review, b21; Schulz 2025, b19).
agent_relevance: For an LLM scaffold the lesson is the menu, not the label: give counts out of N and let code do the one-step ratio. That is what code-side normalisation already does.

source: Macmillan-Scott & Musolesi (2024) (Ir)rationality and cognitive biases in large language models (Royal Society Open Science; arXiv 2402.09193)
finding: Seven LLMs (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Bard, Claude 2, Llama 2 7b/13b/70b) got 12 cognitive-psychology tasks, each prompted 10 times, zero-shot. One task is the Eddy HIV problem (inverse conditional probability), with a Gigerenzer-style facilitated version. The facilitated HIV version was answered correctly more often by all models except Llama 2. On the other facilitated tasks the classic version did better.
numbers: Seven models x 12 tasks x 10 runs. Classic HIV prior 0.01%; facilitated version states natural counts ('out of 10,000 people, 1 person is infected'). Per-model percentages are only in Figure 7, not in the text.
limits: 2023 models only. Zero-shot. Answers were inconsistent over the 10 repeats, and wrong answers were often not human-like. The authors suspect training contamination for classic tasks.
agent_relevance: Only LLM evidence I opened that tests a natural-frequency restatement. It helped on the Bayes (HIV) task, so restating prior and likelihood as 'x out of N' is a cheap step before the update. It did not help on other facilitated tasks.

source: Chen, Jörke, Goliński, Fedzechkina, Sapiro, Williamson, Foti (2026) LLMs are not (consistently) Bayesian (arXiv 2605.06915v2), main results
finding: Full text read. Four multiple-choice evidence tasks (Animals with 500 questions, Political Ideology, MediQ, Eleusis). Two ways to update: BP mode (one piece of evidence at a time, the model's own stated likelihood placed in the prompt, earlier evidence not shown) and batch mode (all evidence at once). BP mode is closer to Bayes. But batch mode gives equal or better task performance, so one-at-a-time with an explicit likelihood does NOT beat batch on accuracy.
numbers: Models: Qwen3-8B/14B, Ministral-8B/14B (reasoning and not), DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B, GPT-4o mini, GPT-5.1 (no reasoning and medium). Weaker models had higher AUROC in batch mode on Animals, Political Ideology and MediQ; stronger models were comparable in both modes; Eleusis showed no difference. ECE was lower in batch mode on the same three datasets. About 70-575 questions per evidence step (Fig. A3).
quote: Fig. 1 shows that weaker models attain higher task performance in batch mode
limits: Measured against the model's OWN stated likelihoods (information-processing gap) plus AUROC and ECE against truth. 8 models, GPT-5.1 the only frontier one; no Claude or Gemini. Steps with under 80% parseable outputs were dropped.
agent_relevance: CORRECTS claim K10. Closer to Bayes is not the same as more accurate. For S7 a per-evidence code posterior is justified for auditability and consistency, not because it raises accuracy.

source: Chen et al. (2026) arXiv 2605.06915v2, sections 4.2-4.5 and discussion: forced Bayes, wrong-direction updates, oracle likelihood
finding: GPT-5.1 was near-optimal Bayesian in BP mode, with and without reasoning, but often far from optimal in batch mode, including moves in the wrong direction relative to its own likelihood. Yet forcing an explicit Bayes posterior from the model's own prior and likelihood did not reliably help, and on MediQ every model would do worse. About half of the batch wrong-direction updates agreed with a better (GPT-5.1) likelihood.
numbers: MediQ: all models would perform worse if explicitly Bayesian. Eleusis: reasoning models (except Ministral 8B-R) worse if forced Bayesian, most other models better. Animals and Political Ideology: no consistent gain. Across datasets except Eleusis, about half of wrong-direction batch updates move toward the oracle likelihood; about 15% more land closer to the oracle posterior. Using the oracle likelihood in explicit Bayes gave 'significant performance gains' where the model's likelihood differed most (App. C.3).
quote: you cannot offload good statistical practice to an LLM
limits: 'Oracle' is GPT-5.1's stated likelihood, a proxy and not ground truth. The Bayes posterior is built from the model's own elicited priors and likelihoods, the weak link. The authors' explanation (training data has many diagnoses, few explicit likelihood tables) is a hypothesis, not tested.
agent_relevance: Answers part of gaps 2 and 6: the stated likelihoods are the weak part, not the arithmetic. The update is only as good as the verbalised P(E|H). Where the model has a strong implicit evidence-to-answer map (medicine), forcing a likelihood table can hurt.

source: Filbry, Melo, Gal (2026) From Prompts to Posteriors: Can LLM agents perform Bayesian inference in context? (arXiv 2610.29331), sections 5-6
finding: Full text read. This paper compares against an EXTERNALLY computed oracle posterior, not only the model's own consistency. Non-reasoning LLMs fail to follow it, which cuts downstream experiment success. Reasoning fixes the simple case. Code execution fixes the case with no closed form.
numbers: 20Q on 40 target animals, T=20 experiments; ProteinWorld: 5 worlds x 8 classes = 40 runs, T=6. Models: Qwen-2.5-32B, Phi-4, Gemma-4-31B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B, Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B (non-reasoning, and reasoning for 3); Gemini-2.5-Pro with Python only on ProteinWorld-hard. Without reasoning, LLM updates cut final success by at least 30% versus the oracle trajectory; some weak models near 0% on 20Q. With reasoning, Gemma-4-31B matched the oracle on ProteinWorld-simple. Hard case (no closed form): high KL; with code execution KL and gap close to 0.
limits: It does NOT test step-by-step versus batch; it tests answer-only vs reasoning vs reasoning plus code. Mostly 26-35B open models. Small N (40 runs per environment). Likelihoods are given or derivable from a known world, unlike open-domain questions.
agent_relevance: Consistent with 'code does the Bayes arithmetic', and measured against truth. Small N, so consistent with, not proof of. Also corrects the critique's worry that b11 only measures self-consistency: it measures distance to an external posterior.

source: Filbry et al. (2026) arXiv 2610.29331, Dutch-book coherence tests (ForecastBench scenarios)
finding: Normalisation (exclusive options summing to 1), monotonicity and extensionality were violated often across separate conversations, much less inside one dialogue where earlier judgments are visible.
numbers: 10 ForecastBench scenarios per violation type, 30 in all, on Gemini-2.5-Pro, Gemma-4-31B-it, Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct. Cross-conversation violation rates exceed 50% of the 30 scenarios for almost all model-constraint pairs. Within one dialogue: about 10% for Gemini and 1 of 30 scenarios for Gemma.
limits: Only 30 scenarios per model; three models, one frontier (Gemini-2.5-Pro, a 2025 model).
agent_relevance: Supports putting the sum-to-1 step in code, not in the prompt: independent elicitation drifts, but showing earlier numbers in the same context repairs most of it.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning, Table 1 aggregation comparison (ICLR; arXiv 2203.11171)
finding: Reopened Table 1 for the 'vote versus normalised probability' question. On PaLM-540B, majority vote and the length-normalised probability-weighted sum agree within 0.3 points. Un-normalised or averaged weighting is clearly worse.
numbers: Accuracy (GSM8K / MultiArith / AQuA / SVAMP / CSQA / ARC-c): greedy 56.5/94.7/35.8/79.0/79.0/85.2; majority vote 74.4/99.3/48.3/86.6/80.7/88.7; weighted sum normalised 74.1/99.3/48.0/86.8/80.7/88.7; weighted sum unnormalised 59.9/92.2/38.2/76.2/76.2/83.5; weighted average normalised 22.1/59.7/15.7/40.5/52.1/51.7.
limits: The weights are sequence probabilities of whole reasoning paths, not verbalised option probabilities, and the model is PaLM-540B (2022). The authors explain the tie: normalised path probabilities are nearly equal. No equal-token comparison against a single stated distribution. No 2025-26 model.
agent_relevance: Once many samples exist, counting votes equals probability weighting, so a code tally of N samples is a safe default. Says nothing about asking one call for a distribution then normalising it. Gap 10 stays open for current models.

source: Balepur, Palta, Rudinger (2024) It's Not Easy Being Wrong: LLMs struggle with process of elimination reasoning (ACL Findings; arXiv 2311.07532)
finding: Compares asking the model to pick the right option with asking it to name the wrong one (eliminate). Elimination was less accurate in every model and dataset. For small models elimination was below the 50/50 guessing level.
numbers: GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613), LLaMA-2 7B/13B/70B, Falcon 7B/40B/180B; 4 datasets (CommonsenseQA, Social IQa, ARC, OpenBookQA); 500 test questions each; 10-shot; cut to 2 choices. Direct answering agrees with itself on repeat more than with elimination, in every model and dataset. The gap narrows as models get bigger. GPT-4 not tested.
limits: Two-option version, 2023 models, few-shot, temperature 0.3. This is one way to produce 'ruled out' calls; it is not the same as grading each option's evidence. Authors suggest pre-training has many explanations of correct options and few of wrong ones.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: LLM 'this one is ruled out' calls are noisier than 'this one is right' calls, and worse for smaller models. A hard zero on such a call carries real error risk. Prefer a small floor or a revive path.

source: Balepur et al. (2024) arXiv 2311.07532, Appendix Table 17: iterative elimination and compounding loss
finding: When the model eliminates options one at a time over 4, 3, then 2 remaining choices, raw accuracy drops each round because a wrongly eliminated gold answer cannot come back.
numbers: ARC, as I read the layout of Table 17 (4, 3, 2 choices, non-CoT): LLaMA-2 70B raw accuracy about .834, .812, .768; LLaMA-2 7B .526, .322, .232. Accuracy conditioned on the gold answer surviving rises (70B: .923 at 2 choices), so the loss is wrong zeros, not harder questions.
limits: Table text extraction was messy; numbers are my reading of the rows and need a check against the PDF before quoting. 2023 open models only. No comparison with soft down-weighting.
agent_relevance: Only measured cost of a wrong zero I found: each hard elimination round costs a few points for a 70B model and 20-30 points for a 7B model. Supports capping eliminations to evidence the model can quote, and keeping eliminated options revivable.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) LLMs are not robust multiple choice selectors, Table 1, Fig. 4, appendix tables (ICLR; arXiv 2309.03882), reopened for permutation-averaging numbers
finding: Position and label bias are real, and averaging over option orderings removes most of it. Cyclic-permutation averaging at 4 times the cost lowered bias and raised accuracy for the 20 models; their cheaper PriDe method gets most of the gain at 1.15 to 3.4 times cost.
numbers: MMLU 0-shot: llama-2-70B default RStd 7.5, accuracy 50.8; cyclic permutation (cost x4) RStd 4.5, accuracy 54.7; PriDe 5% RStd 2.3, accuracy 51.8. llama-30B: 34.6 to 47.7 with cyclic permutation. Moving the gold answer to D lowered gpt-3.5-turbo from 67.2 to 60.9; moving it to A lifted llama-30B from 53.1 to 68.2. Removing option IDs also cut RStd (llama-30B 17.4 to 2.6) but not accuracy.
limits: All 20 models are 2023-era (LLaMA, Vicuna, Llama-2, gpt-3.5-turbo). No 2025-26 frontier test found. Averaging costs K or K! calls unless PriDe-style prior estimation is used.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays OPEN for frontier models. For the scaffold: if option labels are used, shuffle and average the normalised scores over at least a cyclic set, or score options without letter labels.

source: Guda et al. (2025) Quantifying and mitigating selection bias in LLMs (arXiv 2511.21709); Zheng et al. (2026) PA-GRPO (arXiv 2603.21016)
finding: Two 2025-26 papers on selection bias. Both use small or open models, not frontier ones. Guda: majority voting over orderings is effective but costly, so they train a LoRA. PA-GRPO trains for consistency across all permutations.
numbers: Guda 2025: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Phi-2, Llama3.2-3B on ARC, QASC, MedMCQA, TeleQnA, with a permutation bias metric over all orderings. Zheng 2026: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B; 7 benchmarks; consistency checked over all 4!=24 orderings for judge tasks.
limits: Neither tests GPT-5-class, Claude or Gemini. I read setups and abstracts more than full tables, so no per-model effect sizes recorded. PA-GRPO says inference-time debiasing is costly and may hurt reasoning; that is its motivation, not its measurement.
agent_relevance: Selection bias was still being reported for open models of 3-32B in 2025-26. Frontier models remain untested in what I could open.

source: Nafar, Venable, Kordjamshidi (2024) Reasoning over uncertain text by generative LLMs (BLInD; arXiv 2402.09614v3)
finding: Bayesian-network word problems with probabilities written in text. Plain question answering and chain-of-thought do poorly on larger networks. Having the model only extract numbers and write a short probabilistic program that code runs (ProbLog) brings GPT-4 close to perfect.
numbers: BLInD, networks of 2-10 variables. GPT-4 with ProbLog about 98% over V2-10 (96-100% on every split); GPT-4 Basic QA/CoT far lower (about 29% best CoT average, read from a garbled table). Number extraction 100% for GPT-4 on all splits; graph generation 100%.
limits: GPT-3.5, Llama3-8B, GPT-4 (2023-24). Probabilities are given as numbers, so there is no hard step of eliciting likelihoods. Table layout garbled; the CoT figure is approximate.
agent_relevance: Supports the split: model extracts quantities, code multiplies and normalises. Matches S7/G5 design. Not a test of normalising a model-guessed distribution.

source: Schrader, Lange, Razniewski, Friedrich (2024) QUITE: quantifying uncertainty in natural language text in Bayesian reasoning scenarios (arXiv 2410.10449)
finding: Real-world style Bayesian-network questions with categorical variables, numeric or word-of-estimative-probability premises. GPT-4-Turbo and open models are weak, especially on evidential and explaining-away (backward) questions. A fine-tuned parser plus an exact solver is far better.
numbers: Without premises GPT-4 solves only 3.1% of instances. Fine-tuned Mistral-7B + ProbLog answers about every second question correctly. CausalCoT helped GPT-4 and Llama-3 only slightly. With word premises (e.g. 'improbable'), GPT-4 reaches the correct value in 8.7% of cases and ProbLog-FT ties it. GPT-4 prompted to write ProbLog had about 76% parse errors.
limits: GPT-4-Turbo 2024-04 and small open models. Verbal probability words map only loosely to numbers.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 partial: given likelihoods as words, tested models do poorly, and backward inference is where they fail most. Use numbers or a fixed word-to-number table, and let code do the backward step.

source: Nori, Daswani, Kelly et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models (MAI-DxO; arXiv 2506.22405)
finding: A scaffold with a 'Dr. Hypothesis' role that keeps a probability-ranked differential and updates probabilities 'in a Bayesian manner after each new finding' scored higher than the same base model alone, in a sequential case setting.
numbers: 304 NEJM cases. Off-the-shelf o3 78.6% at $7,850 per case; MAI-DxO (o3, no budget) 81.9% at $4,735; max-accuracy configuration 85.5%; generalist physicians 20% average. Single vs batched test ordering for MAI-DxO (o3), 56-case test set: same accuracy 83.9%, cost $3,991 vs $5,084.
limits: Five roles (hypothesis, test chooser, challenger, cost, checklist); no ablation isolates the Bayesian-probability role. The LLM states the probabilities; no code posterior. The single/batched ablation is about ordering tests, not updating beliefs.
agent_relevance: A frontier-model scaffold with a verbalised running differential gained 3.3 points over the base model, but nothing isolates the Bayes part. Not proof for conditionalization.

source: Gupta, Corona, Ge, Wang, Klein, Darrell, Chan (2025) Enough Coin Flips Can Make LLMs Act Bayesian (arXiv 2503.04722v2), reopened for the stated-prior question
finding: Re-read for gap 9. Stating the bias in the prompt is weak for base models and better for instruction-tuned ones. Demonstrations in context outweigh the stated bias. The remaining error is in the starting prior, not the update.
numbers: Biased coin flips; N=50 prompts per condition. Base models ignore biasing instructions and almost always generate a biased distribution (about 70% heads). Instruction-tuned models attend to the stated bias better and do much better at extreme bias (always heads or tails). Best-fit discount value across models runs from about 0.31 (Gemma-2-2B-Instruct) to 0.91 (Mistral-7B-Instruct).
limits: All models at most about 8B. No frontier model, so 'do frontier models move as Bayes predicts when the prior is stated' is untested here. Coin flips are an easy toy task.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays OPEN for frontier models. Practical rule: put the prior in a number the code uses, not only in the prompt.
